artifacts.summary: Research report summarizing the four live measurements and citing the decision record they produced.

The task's named deliverable: a measurement record stating each of the four harness behaviours the amending record's R2 siting depends on, with the exact command/tool call that produced each result, and a verdict that none refutes the siting.

next_steps: Run /orchestrate 668 to create an implementation plan, or proceed directly with the dependent successor tasks (669-675), which were already waiting on this measurement.

memory_candidates.content: guard-destructive-git.sh's destructive-command safety check is anchored to the primary project tree's own git status regardless of a Bash command's own cd target -- confirmed in both directions live: it wrongly allows a destructive command aimed at a dirty external worktree when the primary tree is clean (prior finding), and it wrongly blocks a safe destructive-pattern command aimed at a provably clean external worktree when the unrelated primary tree is dirty (this task's own live reproduction: committed the worktree clean, then ran `cd <clean external worktree> && git reset --hard HEAD` in one Bash call and had it blocked citing the primary tree's uncommitted changes). Any two-root hook fix must repoint this anchor at the actual command target, not patch one direction only.

Path-scoped .claude/rules/*.md `paths:` frontmatter does not match a file whose touched path lies outside the session's own project directory, even when the glob (e.g. lua/**/*.lua) would otherwise match the path's trailing segments. Confirmed by a same-session A/B: the first touch of a matching path this session (an external git-worktree file) produced no rule reminder; the very next touch of the same glob, now in-project, triggered the reminder immediately (including on a nonexistent in-project path, ruling out read-success as the trigger). A worktree of the same repository carries the identical rule file content, so this only affects whether path-scoped guidance is surfaced while editing files that happen to live in the worktree -- a usability cost, not a correctness defect.

A dispatched subagent's Bash tool cwd always resets to the primary project directory between separate tool calls -- never to wherever a prior call's own `cd` left it, and never to any worktree, even when a real external git worktree exists for the whole session. Confirmed twice independently (the dispatching agent itself, and a freshly spawned, context-free general-purpose subagent asked to run the identical three-call pwd/cd-pwd/pwd sequence). Any two-root design must therefore carry the worktree path explicitly (dispatch-file field, script argument) rather than relying on an ambient cwd switch.

user_decision.question: File-tool (Read/Edit/Write) behaviour for a path outside the project directory was measured only under bypassPermissions, the one mode this system's dispatched agents could be shown to run under from static configuration. Does /orchestrate (or any agent dispatch) ever run from a session not started with --dangerously-skip-permissions, and if so, what happens when a subagent's tool call targets a path outside the project directory under that mode?
options: Confirm /orchestrate dispatches always run under bypassPermissions (--dangerously-skip-permissions) in this environment; no further measurement needed.

Report that a non-bypass interactive mode is sometimes used for a dispatch, and describe (or let a future interactive session observe) what the file-tool prompt looks like for an external path under that mode.
user_decision.recommended: Confirm /orchestrate dispatches always run under bypassPermissions (--dangerously-skip-permissions) in this environment; no further measurement needed.
